summary.en: Some short place phrases contain a preposition and an article together.

body.en:
From season 1, episode 1.

Cécile says *à mon cours d'équitation*; the people waiting for her are *au Westin*. Both phrases locate someone, but their following noun phrases are built differently.

*au* combines *à + le*. *aux* combines *à + les*. Before a feminine noun, *à la* remains two words; before a suitable vowel sound you can meet *à l'*. A possessive such as *mon* already determines its noun, so the phrase does not also insert *le* before it.

Learn the location phrase with its noun. Do not infer that every English “at” must always become *au*, or that a named place takes the same article as every other named place.

On replay, compare what follows *à* with what follows *au*. The article is part of the small word you hear, even when there is no separate syllable for it.
